venues.n: Four Seasons Hotel Cairo at Nile Plaza
venues.d: The surest hands in the city — a Nile-front tower where nothing is left to chance.

venues.n: Four Seasons Hotel Cairo at the First Residence
venues.a: Giza (Nile-side, near the zoo & botanical gardens)
venues.d: A stately, residential Four Seasons above the First Mall — grand, calm and quietly grown-up.
The pyramids filling your window from forty acres of gardens — the most storied address in Egypt.
Butler service and gilded Nile-front glamour — the maison's Egyptian flagship.
A polished Ritz-Carlton on the Nile, steps from Tahrir and the old Egyptian Museum.
An island tower ringed by the Nile on three sides — French art de vivre with the river at every window.
A boutique Nile house of butler service and old-world calm, a notch quieter than the towers.
Art-deco grandeur near the airport — the grand hotel for arrivals, departures and business.
A sleek modern Nile-front tower with a landmark rooftop pool over the river.
A resort-scaled Marriott on the city's eastern edge — golf, spa and space to spread out.
A dependable Nile-front business house — capable, central and easy on the bill.
Modern Egyptian cooking at the foot of the Great Pyramid — the finest table in the country, with the view to match.
Elevated Egyptian street food — koshary, ta'ameya and baladi bread, done with colour and real care.
Contemporary Japanese cooking with real precision — the city's most serious sushi and robata.
Confident Mediterranean cooking, warm service and a proper wine list — a striking evening out.
The Giza-side Sachi — the same polished Mediterranean cooking, on the west bank.
A lively Japanese izakaya doing small plates and skewers with genuine intent.
Charcoal-grilled Japanese skewers from the acclaimed kushiyaki name — small food, big flavour.

venues.n: The Pyramids of Giza & the Great Sphinx
venues.d: The last surviving Wonder of the ancient world, and the one sight that hushes even seasoned travellers. Arrange a private Egyptologist and enter at opening, or before it, so the plateau is yours in the cool morning light rather than shared with the coach crowds and the midday heat. The interior of the Great Pyramid and the panorama point beyond the Sphinx are worth the extra tickets.

venues.n: Dawn camel or Arabian-horse ride across the plateau
venues.d: The most cinematic way to first see the pyramids — riding in from the desert side at sunrise, when the light is gold and the plateau is still empty. A good operator brings well-kept Arabian horses rather than the tired camels near the gate, and multi-generation families can go at a gentle walk. Photographers get the frame everyone wants before the crowds arrive.

After dark the Sphinx 'narrates' the story of the pyramids while lasers and coloured light play across the monuments — unashamedly theatrical, but a memorable evening for children and grandparents. Shows run nightly in rotating languages; a discreet private terrace or a nearby rooftop table lets you watch in comfort with dinner.

The largest archaeological museum in the world, opened in full in November 2025 beside the pyramids, and now the single most important museum visit in Egypt. The complete Tutankhamun collection is shown together for the first time since its discovery, and the vast atrium staircase of colossi is breathtaking. Entry is timed and online-only — book well ahead and take a private guide to make sense of 100,000 objects.

The grand old 1902 museum on Tahrir Square, still holding tens of thousands of masterpieces — Middle Kingdom, Late Period and Greco-Roman treasures, jewellery, papyri and coffins — even as Tutankhamun has moved to the GEM. The faded, cabinet-crammed halls have a scholarly romance the new museum can't replicate. Best paired with the GEM over two days, not one.

venues.n: The National Museum of Egyptian Civilization (NMEC) — the Royal Mummies
venues.d: Home to the hushed, reverent Royal Mummies Hall, where 22 pharaohs and queens — Ramses II, Seti I, Hatshepsut among them — lie in a specially designed climate-controlled gallery. It is a genuinely moving, dignified experience rather than a spectacle. The wider museum traces Egyptian civilisation from prehistory to today, and is calm and rarely crowded.

venues.n: The Citadel of Saladin & Mosque of Muhammad Ali
venues.d: Saladin's 12th-century hilltop fortress crowned by the Ottoman-style alabaster Mosque of Muhammad Ali, whose silver domes and twin pencil minarets dominate the skyline. From the ramparts you look clear across the medieval city to the pyramids on a clear day. Go late afternoon for the light and cooler air; modest dress and slip-off shoes for the mosque.

The masterpiece of Mamluk architecture — a colossal 14th-century mosque and school whose soaring stone courtyard and towering iwan leave most visitors silent. It stands facing Al-Rifa'i across a small square, and the pair together is one of Cairo's great architectural set-pieces. A private guide unlocks the geometry and the history of the sultans buried within.

The younger neighbour of Sultan Hassan, completed in 1912 but built to echo Mamluk grandeur, and the royal mausoleum of Egypt's last kings — as well as the tomb of the last Shah of Iran. The marble-and-gilt interior is unexpectedly opulent. Visited together with Sultan Hassan on one ticket, it makes the finest hour of Islamic architecture in the city.

Founded in 970 AD, one of the oldest continuously operating universities in the world and the spiritual heart of Sunni Islam. The serene marble courtyard and layered minarets from different centuries reward a slow, quiet visit. It sits at the entrance to the old city, a natural start to a walk down Al-Muizz Street.

The oldest mosque in Cairo surviving in its original form, from 879 AD — vast, austere and almost empty, with a rare spiral minaret you can climb for a sweeping rooftop view over the old city. Its serene scale is a complete contrast to the bustle outside. Next door, the little Gayer-Anderson Museum occupies two restored merchant houses worth a look.

A pedestrianised open-air museum of medieval architecture — one of the densest concentrations of Islamic monuments anywhere, from the Qalawun complex to Bayt al-Suhaymi. Walk it in the evening when the sabils and minarets are floodlit and the heat has gone. A knowledgeable guide turns a beautiful stroll into a thousand years of history.

The great medieval souk, a warren of alleys selling silver, brass, lanterns, spices and perfume oils since the 14th century. Bargaining is expected and part of the theatre; a guide keeps the touts at bay and takes you to the honest workshops behind the tourist front. Pause for mint tea at the storied El Fishawy café, open more or less continuously for two centuries.

A gift of the Aga Khan built on what was five centuries of rubble, now a serene hilltop garden of formal terraces, fountains and a serpentine lake — with the finest panorama of every minaret in Islamic Cairo. The Citadel View restaurant at sunset is one of the loveliest tables in the city. A green, cooling pause in the middle of a dense day.

The most beloved of Cairo's ancient churches, suspended above a gatehouse of the Roman Babylon fortress, its nave seeming to float over the ruins. The dark wooden ceiling shaped like Noah's Ark and the inlaid pulpit are exquisite. The heart of the compact Coptic quarter, walkable in an easy morning.

The oldest synagogue in Egypt, on a site linked by tradition to where the infant Moses was found, and famous among scholars for the Cairo Geniza — a treasury of a millennium of medieval manuscripts discovered in its loft. Small, atmospheric and beautifully restored. A poignant marker of Cairo's layered Jewish, Christian and Muslim history, all within a few steps.

The world's finest collection of Coptic art — textiles, icons, carved wood and early Christian manuscripts — housed in a jewel-box building with mashrabiya screens and painted ceilings. Quieter and gentler than the pharaonic museums, and a revealing bridge between ancient Egypt and the Christian age. An hour here deepens the whole Coptic quarter.

One of the oldest churches in Cairo, built over a crypt where tradition holds the Holy Family sheltered during their flight into Egypt. Simple, ancient and deeply venerated, it draws pilgrims as much as tourists. A short, meaningful stop on the Coptic circuit, especially for Christian travellers.

The oldest and most graceful way onto the river — a lateen-sailed felucca, chartered privately, drifting past Zamalek and the city skyline as the sun drops. No engine, no music, just the water and the light. The most peaceful hour in Cairo, and lovely for families or a quiet couple's evening.

For an evening with more occasion, a dinner cruise glides past the illuminated city with dinner and, on the classic boats, a whirling-dervish tanoura show and belly dance. Choose a discreet premium operator or charter privately; ask ahead and the galley will happily lay on a full vegetarian or Jain menu. A crowd-pleaser across the generations.

The 187-metre lattice tower on Gezira Island, its openwork concrete inspired by a lotus stem, gives the best 360-degree view of the whole sprawl of Cairo and the Nile threading through it. Go for late afternoon and stay for the lights coming on. A quick, easy orientation for a first day in the city.

Cairo's leafy island district is where the contemporary art scene lives — spaces like Gypsum, Ubuntu and the long-running Zamalek Art Gallery, alongside villa-lined streets, the Aisha Fahmy palace and good cafés. A civilised half-day for collectors and anyone wanting the modern city rather than the ancient one. Easily paired with lunch and a wander.

One of the greatest collections of Islamic art in the world — woodwork, metal, glass, ceramics and carpets spanning the whole Muslim world — beautifully re-displayed after restoration. Far less visited than the pharaonic museums, so it's calm and unhurried. Essential for anyone who falls for the artistry of Islamic Cairo and wants to understand it.

The eccentric, gorgeous early-20th-century palace of Prince Mohamed Ali Tewfik, a magpie's mix of Ottoman, Moorish, Persian and Rococo set in a botanical garden on Rhoda Island. Gilded halls, tiled kilns and a throne room, and rarely crowded. A hidden gem for those who've done the headline sights and want something quieter and unexpectedly lavish.

venues.n: The City of the Dead (Northern Cemetery)
venues.d: A vast living necropolis where centuries of Mamluk mausolea stand among a community that has made homes among the tombs — best seen respectfully and only with a sensitive local guide who has standing there. The soaring funerary complexes of Qaitbay and Barquq are architectural marvels. A profound, humane glimpse of a Cairo few visitors reach; never treat it as a spectacle.

Egypt's essence trade goes back to the pharaohs, and a proper old atelier will sit you down with tiny bottles of jasmine, lotus, sandalwood and 'secret of the desert' over tea. A charming, low-pressure hour — buy the pure oils, skip the alcohol-based blends. Fun for the whole party, and a fragrant, packable gift to take home.

A short, genuine demonstration of how papyrus is beaten, soaked and pressed into a sheet — best at a reputable institute rather than a roadside shop, where the art is real and the paintings are hand-done on true papyrus, not banana leaf. Children love the hands-on part. A tasteful, authentic souvenir when you buy from the right place.

On the road out to Saqqara, family carpet schools show children and weavers at the looms turning wool and silk into hand-knotted rugs and tapestries. It's a window into a craft as much as a shop, and a discreet guide will steer you to the honest houses with fair prices. Serious buyers can commission and ship.

venues.n: Dahshur — the Bent & Red Pyramids (day trip)
venues.d: Two of the most important pyramids in Egypt and among the least crowded: the Bent Pyramid, where the builders changed the angle mid-construction, and the Red Pyramid, the first true smooth-sided pyramid — which you can usually enter with barely another soul inside. Combined with Saqqara and Memphis, it is the finest pyramid day beyond Giza.

A dramatic limestone canyon on the very edge of the city near leafy Maadi, laced with fossils and easy walking trails through the desert quiet — a genuine escape barely half an hour from downtown. Go early for the cool and the light. A refreshing morning of nature for those who want to stretch their legs between the museums.

A startling Hindu-temple-inspired mansion in the garden suburb of Heliopolis, built by a Belgian industrialist and long shrouded in ghost stories, now beautifully restored with a museum on the city's making. Its Angkor-and-Cambodia-styled towers are unlike anything else in Cairo. A quirky, elegant stop that intrigues Indian travellers in particular.

The great southern gate of Fatimid Cairo, from 1092, whose twin minarets you can climb for one of the finest close-up views over the roofs, domes and minarets of the old city. The Tentmakers' market (Khayamiya) with its hand-appliquéd fabrics runs just beside it. A rewarding climb and a living craft street, away from the main crush.

El Fishawy, tucked in the lanes of Khan el-Khalili, has poured mint tea and shisha for some 250 years beneath its mirrored walls — a favourite of the Nobel laureate Naguib Mahfouz. Sit, watch the alley theatre, and let the sweet-tea sellers and rose-water hawkers come to you. The most atmospheric pause in the old city.

The spinning Sufi tanoura at the restored Wikala of al-Ghuri is hypnotic — a spiritual dance of skirts and colour rather than a tourist floor-show, staged in a beautiful Mamluk caravanserai. Free or very low cost, and mesmerising for children. A gentle, uplifting evening in the heart of the medieval city.

Egyptian cooking is a joy for vegetarians — koshari (the beloved lentil-rice-pasta bowl), ful medames, taameya (Egyptian falafel of fava beans), fresh mango and sugar-cane juices. A private guide takes you to the best, cleanest tables and can arrange strictly veg or Jain-aware stops. Delicious, sociable, and revealing of the real Cairo.

venues.n: A hot-air balloon is Luxor — instead, a helicopter or private-plane extension
venues.d: For travellers with only days, a private-plane or fast-flight extension pairs Cairo with Luxor and Aswan — the temples of Karnak, the Valley of the Kings and a Nile dahabiya — without losing time to long drives. Your concierge sequences it as one seamless journey. The natural next chapter once Cairo's wonders are done.

Cairo layers Roman, Coptic, Fatimid, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman stone within a few square kilometres — a photographer's dream of mashrabiya screens, spiral minarets, painted ceilings and carved domes. A dawn walk with a guide who knows the light and the caretakers gets you inside courtyards before they open. Endlessly rewarding for anyone who loves buildings.

Two joined 16th- and 17th-century merchant houses beside the Ibn Tulun mosque, filled by a British collector with Ottoman furniture, mashrabiya balconies and secret passages — a perfectly preserved window into old domestic Cairo (and a James Bond film set). Small, atmospheric and easily combined with the mosque next door. A charming hidden gem.

venues.n: The Nilometer & Umm Kulthum Museum, Rhoda
venues.d: At the southern tip of Rhoda Island, the elegant 9th-century Nilometer once measured the river's flood that decided Egypt's fortunes, beside a small museum to Umm Kulthum, the beloved 'Star of the East'. A quiet, offbeat pairing of ancient science and modern legend. A short, cultured stop for those who like the corners others miss.

venues.n: The Roof — Four Seasons Cairo at Nile Plaza
venues.d: An open-air bar high above the Nile at the city's most exacting hotel — the drink with the finest river view.
An eleventh-floor rooftop over the Nile and the skyline — a calm, grown-up nightcap above the city.
